title: Mamluk Cairo
hook: former slave-soldiers rule Egypt and build mosques, hospitals and schools

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Tusi's observatory on a hilltop at Maragha, paid for by a Mongol prince. Your line was learning survived.

A boy is sold in a market far from home, somewhere on the grasslands north of the Black Sea, and shipped to Egypt. There he is taught Arabic, the Qur'an and prayer, then the horse, the bow and the lance. When his training ends, he is freed and becomes a soldier of the sultan. That was the path of the mamluks. Some who walked it became sultans themselves, ruling Egypt from the citadel above Cairo. And then they started to build. Today: Mamluk Cairo.
screen: `A BOY SOLD FAR FROM HOME.` → `TRAINED, THEN FREED.` → `SOME BECAME SULTANS.`

segments.voice: In Arabic, mamluk means one who is owned. These were children bought and taken from their families. Nothing in today's story makes that good. What the story shows is what some of them did once they held power. They built. Walk down the old main street of Cairo today and their buildings still stand shoulder to shoulder: mosques, schools, fountains, tombs. Sultan Qalawun, once a mamluk himself, built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital, a bimaristan, side by side. The endowment that paid for the hospital, as historians describe it, was meant for anyone who was sick, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge. Later, his grandson Sultan Hasan, born a prince rather than bought, built a great mosque and college, with space for teaching the different schools of Sunni law under one roof. Why build like this? Partly for memory and standing, like rulers anywhere. But there's a teaching underneath, taught in the very schools they built. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except three: a charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A hospital is a charity that keeps on giving. A school is knowledge still in use. Men who had once been owned, and their heirs, may well have been thinking about what they would leave behind when they owned nothing again. Slaves became builders. People still pray in some of those mosques.
screen: `MAMLUK — ONE WHO IS OWNED.` · `QALAWUN: A TOMB, A SCHOOL, A HOSPITAL.` · `SULTAN HASAN'S MOSQUE AND COLLEGE.` · `THREE DEEDS THAT DON'T END.` · then, large: `SLAVES BECAME BUILDERS.`

segments.voice: Think of the oldest building you can get to, a mosque, a church, a library, a bridge, and picture yourself at its door. Look for what a hurried visitor misses, a step worn hollow by feet, a patch where the stone was mended, and ask what it was built to do and what it does now. If you pray, ask that whatever good it still does keep going; if not, simply hold it in mind.
Mamluk Cairo. The city ruled by former slave-soldiers, who filled it with mosques, schools and hospitals that still stand. Today's words.
Your line: slaves became builders. A hospital, a school: deeds that keep going. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, and some give to build or keep up mosques, schools, wells and hospitals in the hope that the good continues after them.

chat.says: Why did Cairo's Mamluk sultans build so many hospitals and schools?
options: A hadith says lasting charity and useful knowledge keep giving after death.
Because the law required every sultan to build at least one hospital.
To hide that they had once been slaves, so that no one would ask.
chat.meaning: A hadith in Sahih Muslim: a person's deeds end at death except a lasting charity, useful knowledge, and a righteous child who prays for them.

mamluk.meaning: one who is owned; a freed slave-soldier

Qalawun.meaning: a mamluk who became sultan and built a hospital

Sultan Hasan.meaning: Qalawun's grandson, builder of a great mosque and college

Sultan Hasan's complex as housing teaching in the four Sunni schools of law ('the different schools'); confirm.
